title: Rebbe Nachman's practice: go outside and talk
hook: Rebbe Nachman's practice: go outside and talk
tomorrow: the day the whole people says sorry together

segments.voice: Yesterday: kavanah, aiming your heart where your words are going. Your line was mean it. Did one autopilot phrase get meant? Day fifteen.

Night, outside a small town in Ukraine. Out past the last houses, in a field, a man is walking alone among the grass. He isn't reading from a book. He isn't singing a set prayer. He's talking. Out loud, in plain Yiddish, the language of his kitchen, the way you'd talk to a friend you trust: about his day, his worries, what he's ashamed of, what he wants. Anyone passing might think he's lost his mind. He's doing exactly what his teacher told him to do. Today: the rabbi who sent people outside to talk.
screen: `A FIELD AT NIGHT.` → `A MAN TALKING OUT LOUD.` → `NO BOOK, NO SET WORDS.`

segments.voice: The teacher was Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, a Hasidic master. The practice is called hitbodedut, from a Hebrew root that means alone. Making yourself alone. Rebbe Nachman taught that besides the fixed prayers, the ones in the prayer book, a person should set aside time every day, an hour if possible, to speak to God in their own words and their own language. Not Hebrew, if Hebrew isn't how you talk. Whatever language your heart actually uses. Best of all in a field or a forest, among the grass, where, he said, every blade joins in. And he was practical about the hard days. If you can't find anything to say, he taught, then say that. Tell God you can't find the words. Even repeating one phrase, over and over, like master of the world, counts. The point isn't eloquence. The point is showing up and opening your mouth. Jewish tradition finds a hint of it in the Torah. In Genesis, Isaac, Abraham's son, is described this way in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." The rabbis read that as Isaac praying, outside, at the end of the day. Breslov Hasidim still practice hitbodedut, often at night, often outdoors, and other Jews have taken it up too. It sits right next to yesterday's word. The fixed prayers give you words to mean. Hitbodedut asks you to mean words that are entirely your own.
screen: `REBBE NACHMAN OF BRESLOV.` · `HITBODEDUT — MAKING YOURSELF ALONE.` · `IF YOU CAN'T SPEAK, SAY THAT.` · `ISAAC WENT OUT INTO THE FIELD.` · then, large: `IN YOUR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell, and this one uses your voice. If you can, speak out loud, even in a whisper. If you pray, talk to God the way Rebbe Nachman taught: plainly, in your own words, about whatever is actually on your mind. If you don't pray, say out loud what's on your mind anyway, as if to a friend who's listening. If nothing comes, say that nothing comes. The bell holds the time.
Hitbodedut. Making yourself alone, to talk to God out loud in your own words. Fifteenth word.
Your line: talk to him out loud. Today, find five minutes alone, a walk, a car, a quiet room, and speak what's on your heart, out loud, in your own words. Day fifteen.

screen: `DAY 15 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DAY THE WHOLE PEOPLE SAYS SORRY TOGETHER.`

howItsDone: Breslov Hasidim, and some other Jews, practice hitbodedut by going somewhere alone, often outdoors at night, and speaking to God aloud in their own language for a set time each day.

original.note: Hebrew: making oneself alone, from the root b-d-d, alone.

trapdoor: what you thought: some kind of meditation.
what it means: going off alone every day to talk to God out loud, in your own words and language.
what a scholar hears: Likutey Moharan II:25 sets out the practice; Rebbe Nachman read Isaac's 'meditating in the field' (Genesis 24:63) as prayer.
